SUMMARY
ACTIONS
GRR LTD has been commissioned to inspect the green roof at Purley Court. No maintenance was instructed. The
roof inspection was undertaken using licenced & insured drone. 

SUMMARY
OBSERVATIONS
The vegetation is in good condition, benefitting from the mixture of sunshine during summer months and recent
showers. Plant communities appera healthy with coverage very good. 
Some moss areas remain (top left)
Some repairs to masonry on chimneys have been effected but some remain unaddressed (below left)
Some stones dislodged by wind are visible on the waterproofing outside of the perimeter alu to all sides car park/side
road (top right)

SUMMARY

Relocate stones displaced by wind/birds
Add ballast to dislodged modules, or re-install properly on new drainage boards properly ballasted with exting
material to remove the air gaps 
Please advise if you wish GRR to quote for any of these works

OVERVIEW
WATERPROOFING
GRR was invited to inspect the green roof at 147 De Beauvoir, where water is presenting internally in multiple
 locations below the first floor extension. Ingress was first reported in [tbc]. Earlier efforts by builders onsite t
o ascertain cause involved soil stack and overlay in PVC to valley gutter and garden-side lip.

There are number of possible weak points all along the curved upstand behind the vertical cladding, however no
 obvious source of ingress here was found during the inspection. Full excavation is recommended to allow eithe
r any specific flaws to be exposed and remedied, and/or overlay of all joints (see below left). A flaw was noted 
in the seal at the end of the valley gutter, which should be addressed (below right). There is a mastic only seal
 at the abutment of metal coping and masonry (bottom left). This should have a proper flashing detail.  

FINDINGS
WATERPROOFING cont
On the steeply pitched side there multiple welded straps which have been used to secure green roof material.
 There is evidence that during the welding there has been damage to the membrane below - see marks from wel
d gun nozzle and small hole (below left). If there are many of these welds in this area as appears to be the ca
se (below right), this is a candidate for some of the leaks. We have recently observed and rectified exactly this on a 
rood for Brighton and Hove Council.

FINDINGS
GREEN ROOF BUILD UP
The green roof is an improvised combination of methods which appears to have worked adequately in some
 areas  but  is  overall  not  performing  to  the  standards  of  finish  observed  elsewhere.  The  roof  will  need  to  b
e cleared back around 1m away from  the building and entire length of steeper side. Reinstating is not worth it 
on the steep side and depending how continuous the planting finish should be, it may be better to start again w
ith the planting all over. However, the growing medium may well be reusable   than expected over its long life, and 
section of it should continue to survive if left as is with tweaks to the care regime.
The most important consideration once waterproofing is resolved is the absence of clarity on anti-shear
 methods  to  the  steeper  side.  Thought  will  need  to  be  given  by  chosen  installer  to  both  the  mismatch  i
n appearance between locally relaid areas and the existing roof run, and the need to add verifiably secure ant
i-shear measures to those areas which are relaid. 
The green roof should be brought away from the house by minimum 150mm to reduce risk of ingress, and the
 ingress of growing medium rectifed to prevent root growth near joints. Filling this cleared area with stones i
s optional , an d though t ma y b e give n t o a versio n o f th e Shingl e Roo f whic h esche s aluminiu m an d creat
es naturalistic stones swirls and channels around the reused substrate 
If the area around the large skylight now overrun with grass is considered unsightly, this can be lifted and
 disposed, and replaced with a suitable contemporary pitched green roof build up in accordance with good green 
roof practice and manufacturers instructions.
Thankfully there is no need to have scaffold for any of the proposed works, which could be done safely without.

RECOMMENDATIONS
A REPAIR
When identifying cause of water ingress, the process is one of elimination of possible explanations in order of
likelihood. For this reason, we like to see fairly obvious explanations in the immediate vicinity of the
staining/dripping (apart from particular types properties eg Passivhaus which have good quality materials
providing airtightness that can carry water in many directions, in most case water tends to present below the
issue or close to it). 
Where potential candidates are discovered in region of leaks, localised repairs may be considered. This involves
removing green roof elements, setting aside if they have value/are worth saving (replacing if not) and
cleaning/preparing for suitable repair material. 
This may be considered in this case, to approx 1m strip of the roof from side to side around upper floor upstands.
Please note that this work is intended to eliminate most likely causes, and no warranty beyond materials
guarantee can be given in respect of further leaks, ie that other leaks will not develop elsewhere or that this
work has indeed caught all of the issues currently present.
STEP BY STEP
Clear all green roof materials to ground level and set aside for reuse that which can be saved. Budgetary
 provision should be made for replacement with modern equivalents as required. Disposal of remainder wit
h local licenced waste contractor. 
1.
Clean down roof and prepare for overlaying in suitable material in line with manufacturer instructions to
 enable a warranty to be offered on the finish. 
2.
Conduct repairs generally as described above, overlay roof in suitable membrane in line with good roofing 
practice and obtain IBG (insurance backed) warranty if possible (for full overlay).
3.
Reinstate salvageable green roof components and complement with suitable quality retention layer and 
planting. Reconnect/add irrigation.
4.
Maintain in line with good green roof practice 
5.
Where a full warranty is required, it is necessary for a full overlay. This includes stripping off green roof as
above, and a full recoat by a waterproofing company to whom we will make an introduction for them to consider
pricing. Any company can undertake this, however they should ensure their warranty includes green roof
installation by 3rd party if reinstatement is your prerefence/obligation.

The build up of the green roof is a loose-laid extensive green roof substrate of unknown provenance. There is a
 significant proportion of sandy loam combined with chippings and vermiculite or equivalent lightweight mass. The depth appears to be inadequate at 30-40mm, sitting over a drainage board with integrated filter.
In the roof adjacent to the hotel there is and additional pile of builders sand intended as habitat for solitary
 bees, which has increased the depth by an additional 50mm or so. Logs have been laid loosely on some of the 
roofs.
Planting in all areas is poor, with moss prevalent and occasional invasive prospering in the shadier areas or near
 outlets. 
OVERVIEW
WATERPROOFING
GRR was invited to inspect the green roof at The Hickman, Whitechapel. No ingress has been reported. The
 membrane is exposed in places on vertical upstands, and appears to be in good condition. 
  
VEGETATION

FINDINGS
VEGETATION
i)The build up of the green roof is below that which should be expcted for any green roof, but particularly for one
 client  might  reasonably  expect  to  match  the  quality  of  finishes  elsewhere  in  the  property.  The substrate (growing medium) appears to be non-standard, with an unusual grey hue, sandy consistency and with lots of lightweight filler (vermiculite or equivalent). The presence of moss and little else indicates it is not draining well. This could also be in part a result of the base layers not being of optimal design.
Green roofs are not subject to any regulations except pertaining to fire, and only recently was a British Standard
 brought in for testing growing medium performance in certain respects (water retention, freedom from heav
y metal s etc) . I n orde r t o gro w plant s successfull y i n thes e conditions , i t wil l b e necessar y t o begi n agai
n, disposing of the existing, and introducing deeper and better quality growing media - depth and type depending 
on aesthetic and biodiversity outputs desired from next iteration.
ii)The roof has approx 10% coverage of plants, rising to perhaps 65% if moss is considered. This appears 
reasonably consistent around the building, indicating the problem is not primarily one of aspect.
iii)The presence of moss indicate poor drainage. A combination of elements (blocked outlets, improperly laid
 drainage boards for example) may be contributing to this but the complexion of the growing medium makes thi
s th e mos t likel y candidate . Substrat e ca n b e teste d a t a cos t i f require d t o pursu e rectificatio n fo
rm designer/installe r. Sampl es c an be se nt f or l ab testi ng b ut on ly to advi se wheth er it mee ts t he BS   the erroneous geotextile causing this, but it may also be the falls of the roof structure not allowing the material to drain.  

A) Identify priorities/outcomes: should planting type be optimised for aesthetics, biodiversity contribution
 maintenance implications etc. What is a realistic maintenance footprint? How will the roofs be watered? Are all 
the roofs to be planted identically?
B) Once planting type and watering footprint agreed, confirm depth of substrate required, and match to alu
 separator profile to provide relevant depth retaining function. For example provide 120mm upstand to retai
n 150mm average depth additional material, tapered at edges to 100mm. For sedum, this can reduced by around 
50%.
C) Consider aesthetic & biodiversity enhancements with formal or informal arrangements of natural materials.
 Stone swirls, land-art inspired log piles, habitat panels can balance seasonal changes in flora providing zer
o maintenance year round interest. 
D) Consideration should be given to the time of year work is scheduled. Given lack of easy access to water in
 several locations, Spring and Autumn may be considered optimal. However, the iteration of these planted area
s can give an opportunity to consider successional planting schemes, rejuvenating with new plants periodicall
y. This can open opportunities to provide support to mental health gardening groups and community horticult
ure ther apy initiati ves f rom w ho m a sup ply  of pla nts can  be procur ed. Excell ent narrat ive opportunit ies  in 
this direction, turning these under performing spaces into an opportunity for meaningful community engag
ement and support. 
E) Maintain in line with good green roof practice, as suited to the planting spec chosen by client.
RECOMMENDATIONS
Biodiversity: One Newman St
Roof habitat panels : Hackney

OVERVIEW
The roof is formed from a single lead sheet laid over a plywood deck. There is a cementitious finish on three

ld repair 

SUMMARY
The lead is old and has been repaired once already. The failed repair is the most likely cause of the ingress but
 there is at least one areas where poor material selection could create weak points where ingress is possible. 
The localised re-repair undertaken during visit may be a short term solution but consideration should be given to
 a more substantial intervention. Localised repairs will not provide a warranty against future problems - only 
a new covering can do this. 
The lead is probably at the end of its life and should be updated with another material. When it is removed, the
 deck  and  beams  could  be  thorougly  checked  for  damage  from  ongoing  leaks.  At  this  stage  assessing  th
e structura l strengt h o f th e existin g woul d b e advisabl e i f a ne w gree n roo f i s a preferre d finish . A structur
al engineer is the appropriate professional for confirming the maximum load which can be put on the roof. 
Once the deck and structure have been confirmed suitable for any ancillary works such as green roof, a new
 finish should be applied. Given the constraints imposed by varying masonry finishes, it mayt be advisable to add 
new ply upstands on three sides face fixed to existing masonry to ensure integrity of the waterproofing finish.

 irrigation feed for watering.

Maintain in line with good green roof practice

OVERVIEW
WATERPROOFING
GRR was invited to inspect the green roof at 93 NELSON RD, where water is presenting internally. Ingress was
 first reported in ~2021. No prior efforts to ascertain cause have been made, nor have any interventions bee
n made . Leak s i n evidenc e i n multipl e place s aroun d th e LH S skylight , seale d ven t an d intersectio n wit h side 
return glazing.
VEGETATION
The build up of the green roof above the single ply waterproofing is a loose laid 'system': sedum blankets laid
 directly  onto  loose  substrate  over  a  thin  drainage  layer  with  integral  filter/geotextile  fleece.  There  is  a  thi
n (<100mm ) pebbl e borde r aroun d skyligh t wit h a perforate d aluminimu m edg e supplie d b y Optigreen . T
he pebbl es a re fill ed wi th substra te reduci ng draina ge functio n, a nd the re is no draina ge boa rd r un rig ht up
 to upstands, further negatively reducing rate of egree. 
The roof above drains directly onto the substrate, meaning the planting here has washed away. 

FINDINGS
1 MASONRY
Multiple weak points found in the intersections of roofing work and masonry with overlaps not completed,
 cracked and missing pointing. 

FINDINGS
2 WATERPROOFING
The roof is covered in Hertalan EPDM, a very high quality material but one which is prone to workmanshhip
 issues on changes in angle or complicated details such as penetrations. Exposing the external corner above on
e of the leaks revealed a failure or insufficient application of KS96 sealant. Good practice with this material is 
to leave the area above and adjacent to this kind of non-root proof seal unplanted to avoid root penetration 
and facilitate inspection in event of any issues. The size of the roof has presumably led to the erroneous decision to  plant much close than appropriate. 
The roof was not fully inspected because the workmanship limitations here and with the instersections with
 masonry shown above suggest all 4 corners and the roof vent likely to require rectifying to eliminate risk. 

SUMMARY
There are areas where poor workmanship and material selection have combined to create weak points where
 ingress  is  likely  now  and  in  the  future.  There  are  also  questionable  design  choices  such  as  the  absence  o
f measure s t o facilitat e wate r egres s fro m th e roof s above , an d proximit y o f plantin g t o skyligh t give n t
he waterproofing type. 
Localised uncovering and repairs should be considered (see below). Localised repairs will not provide a warranty
 against future problems - only a new covering can do this. 
The vegetation is not the cause of the leaks: the plants are not tenacious enough to grow through. The quality of
 the vegetation is not super high, and the disruption implied by the works needed to rectify means new plantin
g will be necessary. This is an opportunity to think about how to increase both the aesthetics and the ecological 
function of the roof, as well as considering how to care for the plants to ensure good quality into the future.

RECOMMENDATIONS
A REPAIR
When identifying cause of water ingress, the process is one of elimination of possible explanations in order of
likelihood. For this reason, we like to see fairly obvious explanations in the immediate vicinity of the
staining/dripping (apart from particular types properties eg Passivhaus which have good quality materials
providing airtightness that can carry water in many directions, in most case water tends to present below the
issue or close to it). 
Where potential candidates are discovered in region of leaks, localised repairs may be considered. This involves
removing green roof elements, setting aside if they have value/are worth saving (replacing if not) and
cleaning/preparing for suitable repair material. 
This may be considered in this case and GRR are able to quote for this. Please note that this work is intended to
eliminate most likely causes, and no warranty beyond materials guarantee can be given in respect of further
leaks, ie that other leaks will not develop elsewhere or that this work has indeed caught all of the issues
currently present.
STEP BY STEP
Clear all green roof materials to ground level. The green roof material is not high quality and should be
 evaluated  for  what  is  worth  saving.  Budgetary  provision  should  be  made  for  a  better,  lighter  system
. Disposal of remainder with local licenced waste contractor. 
1.
Clean down roof and prepare for overlaying problem areas in suitable material in line with manufacturer
 instructions to enable a warranty to be offered on the finish. 
2.
Conduct repairs to pointing and masonry generally
3.
Where IBG sought, overlay roof in suitable membrane in line with good roofing practice and as directed by 
manufacturers instructions. Obtain IBG if possible.
4.
Reinstate salvageable green roof components and complement with suitable quality retention layer and
 planting. Ensure that materials are installed in such a way as to be optimised for water egress - with large
r gaps and clear route to outlet for water from roofs above. 
5.
Maintain in line with good green roof practice 
6.
Where a full warranty is required, it is necessary for a full overlay. This includes stripping off green roof as
above, and a full recoat by a waterproofing specialist. It may be necessary to lift the coping stones and skylight
glazing, as well as the lead flashings to achieve a warrantiable seal. Roofing companies should advise
individually on works required to provide a robust and long term warranty with IBG (insurance backed
guarantee)

The green roof is poorly installed, with inadequate and mistakenly layered materials, with sloppy installation
 and signs that there was no watering-in. The build up of the green roof to be 
sedum blanket
thick geotextile placed over the drainage layer instead of underneath
thin sprinkle of a vermiculite-based substrate - around 10-20mm poured into the drainage boards, blocking 
the drainage holes
25mm Optigreen drainage (potential fleece below, not exposed)
Coverage estimate is perhaps around 30%. The plants which have survived are in excellent condition but there
 are  large  areas  of  moss  encroachment,  probably  due  to  the  improper  installation  of  the  substrate  IN  th
e drainage. There is also evidence everywhere of the blankets having shrunk post-installation which is a tell for 
no irrigation. Indeed we were shown area where this is demonstrably unfinished. The irrigation ‘system’ instal
led was incompl ete and ineffecti ve, and evide nce t hat was lik ely sig ned off non-operation al. T hat the r oof
 has survived in the condition it is will in large part be due to good efforts of centre management staff with rea
ctive watering during dry periods. 
WATERPROOFING
GRR was invited to inspect the green roof at Tungate Quarter Shopping Centre. No concerns have been reported
 regarding  waterproofing  and  was  not  inspected  closely.  The  material  appears  to  be  single  ply  welded  sheet 
Sarnafil or equivalent. Any works on the green roof should be approved by warranty/IBG holders.
  
VEGETATION
FINDINGS

FINDINGS
The depth of the substrate appears to a below guidelines average ~10mm except in the area of roof nearest the
 loading point during works, where a significant depth appears to have been achieved in a small area close t
o assume craneage point at time of install. While there are no regulations in this area, good green roof practice 
is to install layers in the correct order and with correct depth of growing medium with irrigation for watering
-in and then reactive support during dry periods. A sample specification doc with indicative images will be supp
lied separately. 
It is surprising and unfortunate that this was not snagged during works or noticed by client’s QC, but it is not
 untypical of the sector. There are an abundance of companies with non-specialists undertaking installation, an
d the absence of regulation means that the techniques, while simple, are largely unknown or ignored.  

FINDINGS
The drainage channels have significant numbers of plants encroaching. While these are only sedum (rather than
 grass) this is not significant issue for the egress of water but should be addressed once or twice a year as par
t of a routine planned maintenance schedule. Such work is not forensic, it does not remove completely, rather 
it should be understood as management. The plants can be easily relocated to the main roof to help with pl
ant coverage in the desired areas.  
There are some inblown invasives, primarily grass, in the area where the substrate intended for the rest of the
 roof appears to have been deposed. Elsewhere these invasives cannot prosper in the poorly installed build-u
p and pose no significant threat to the fabric of the building provided there is a routine maintenance schedule 
in place.  

RECOMMENDATIONS
The green roof has not been installed properly, with inadequate amounts and arrangement of materials. The
 inability of water to drain freely as intended is helping to keep the specimens that do survive in good conditio
n but also encourages an abundance of moss which retards more substantial growth. 
There are three potential pathways here to improve the condition of the roof
A) Key elements of the green roof have been installed incorrectly and the reservoir/drainage boards (often
 called  eggcrates  by  lay  people)  have  been  filled  up  with  growing  medium  by  non-professional  installers
, leavin g the m blocke d an d largel y redundant . Whil e i t i s possibl e t o rectif y an d reus e th e boards , i t wi
ll requi re everythi ng to be lifte d, a nd th is wi ll me an n ew planti ng overlai d. Pa th  A is to  accept blocked drainage, add substrate to gaps, partially scarify moss areas (around 70% of roof) and plant with plants removed from the drainage channels during maintenance. Viability will be enhanced by adding properly designed and installed automated zonal irrigation & maintaining in line with good green roof practice (see attached care agreement)  
B) partial re-installation in areas visible to residents (lift all materials retaining drainage boards for reuse, 
relay new replacement materials in correct order), irrigate & maintain in line with good green roof practice
C) full re-installation (lift all materials retaining drainage boards for reuse, relay new replacement materials 
in correct order), irrigate & maintain in line with good green roof practice

The vegetation is in generally poor condition, consistent with prolonged desiccation following the driest spring
in a century. This is likely exacerbated by compaction, as ineffective drainage leads to fine particles migrating
downward and lightweight aggregate (LECA) rising to the surface. The drainage board in use appears poorly
suited to this context: its perforations are easily obstructed where substrate rests directly against it, limiting
water movement. In wetter periods, this results in episodes of rank growth that then collapse under drought
stress, leaving an unstable and low-performing sward. 
Ecologically, the roof currently offers limited value—floral resources for pollinators are scarce beyond isolated
late-season Valeriana, structural diversity is minimal, and the overall habitat quality appears weak. However,
the site retains potential. With improvements to drainage design and substrate structure, and supported by an
active management regime—such as seasonal cut-and-clear and strategic reintroduction of appropriate plug
plants or seed—it could evolve into a more resilient and ecologically valuable system within two to three years. 
The underlying issue appears to lie in the inability of the roof build-up to shift water at the volume required: the
drainage board installed above the root barrier does not facilitate cross‑flow at a rate consistent with the outlet
design, and the inverted insulation layer further inhibits water from reaching the structural deck, where the
primary egress points are located.

RECOMMENDATIONS
A. MAINTAIN + SEED

dominant colonisers and create space for desirable species to establish. Following this, a trial round of direct
seeding and plug planting (targeted species mix) can be introduced in select areas, ideally after a rain event or
in conjunction with hand-watering. This approach relies heavily on natural rainfall, existing substrate structure,
and gentle seasonal care. While the impact may be modest, this pathway allows for phased adaptation over time
and can be repeated seasonally. It does not solve underlying drainage issues, but can offer small wins in visible
greening and pollinator value, especially in more sheltered roof zones.

For clients seeking a more robust and longer-term outcome, this pathway includes all elements of B, but with
added works to improve underlying conditions: clearing substrate, replacing all existing drainage with fit for

consultation with adjacent Camley Street nature reserve). Additions of varied material types arranged in land
art assemblages to support microhabitats and species diversity while adding narrative and visual interest.
This pathway significantly improves the value of the site and its chances of long-term success, but also brings

extreme droughts; and regular cut/clear cycles will be essential. Success here depends not just on design but

what is normally required to protect the building fabric and to ensure a dependable, warrantied roof finish.

FINDINGS
2. Observed Conditions & Potential Risks
2.1 Lead Flashing & Upstand Detailing
Sections of lead appear to be lifting or curling, possibly through age, movement or insufficient fixing.
Some laps look shallow, irregular, or reliant on sealant, which may have reached the end of its serviceable
life.
There is a high risk of capillary action where water may be drawing behind or beneath the lead due to it its
proximity to water retaining materials and termination on the horizontal (deck).
Certain terminations seem to be bonded onto painted masonry rather than chased into joints, which could
reduce their reliability.
2.2 Masonry Condition
Low-level brickwork displays open joints, friable mortar and possible early spalling.
Voids and soft areas were visible immediately adjacent to the timber frame.
There may have been prolonged moisture loading at this level.
2.3 Timber Frame
Timber surfaces appear weathered, with flaking paint and early softness at the base.
The junction between frame, masonry and lead appears reliant on small patches of aged sealant.

STEP BY STEP

1.Form a 500 mm vegetation-free inspection and maintenance channel along the full length of the abutting
wall.
2.Remove vegetation, loose stone and existing degraded base layers in this zone.
3.Retain stone for potential reuse; assume base layers will require replacement.
PHASE 2 – Masonry & Lead Remediation
1.Carefully clean back the area to expose masonry, waterproofing and lead.
2.Rake out any loose mortar and re-point as needed.
3.Remove aged sealant and any loose or unbonded lead.
4.Re-form the lead flashing to recognised standards:
Chase into brickwork (minimum 75 mm where feasible).
Provide appropriate laps, drips and joints to reduce possible capillary draw.
Ensure a positive pitch away from the wall.
Inspect the underlying waterproofing; local repairs may be needed before reinstatement.
PHASE 3 – Timber Frame Junction
1.Prepare and repair deteriorated timber at the window base (fill, splice, or consolidate as appropriate).
2.Re-prime and redecorate using a suitable microporous coating.
3.Install a more robust flashing termination at the frame/junction, avoiding reliance on silicone alone.

vegetation-free zone from the abutting wall

budgeting purposes clients are often advised to allow for complete replacement.

SUMMARY
This extensive green roof, installed using a Knauf Urbanscape 40mm mineral wool system, is currently showing
significant vegetation loss and substrate stress. Upon inspection, the twin driver of decline appears to be a
infestation of leatherjacket larvae (crane fly larvae), which have undermined sedum root structure over the
winter. This has beenb compounded by calcification of porous pipe irrgation, which released no flow undfer
observation during manual setting. 
Key Findings
1. Leatherjacket Infestation – Primary Concern
 • Widespread presence of crane fly larvae confirmed across multiple zones.
 • Root mass damage visible and consistent with leatherjacket feeding behaviour.
 • Feeding likely intensified over winter and early spring when vegetation was dormant.
2. Vegetation Stress & Dieback
 • Major bare zones observed
 • Residual sedum clusters show desiccation and thinning; some viable material remains.
 • No moss present, indicating low sustained moisture levels.
3. Substrate Surface Condition
 • Crusting and organic fine accumulation noted in bare patches.
 • May have become hydrophobic inhibiting rewetting and promoting further root stress.
4. Irrigation Failure
 • Calcification in porous pipe infrastructure leading to poor water distribution.
 • Current setup not suitable for biological control or uniform rehydration.
5. Actions
1 sack dry biomass removed
feed applied

SUMMARY
Understanding Leatherjackets: Why Now?
Leatherjackets are the larvae of crane flies (Tipula spp.). Adults lay eggs in late summer to early autumn. The larvae:
 • Feed on plant roots through autumn, winter and early spring
 • Are least visible when most active (soil temperatures 5–15°C)
 • Peak damage occurs just as sedum begins new growth (March–April), causing apparent “sudden” collapse
This year’s warm, wet winter followed by an abrupt dry spring has created ideal conditions for high larval survival, but poor plant resilience
— a classic setup for pest-led collapse.
Recommendations
Step 1: Biological Control (local contractor)
 1. Apply Nematodes: Steinernema feltiae
 • Apply with water at dusk when soil temperature >10°C.
 • Focus on zones with visible larvae or bare vegetation.
 • Requires consistent moisture for 3–5 days post-application (see irrigation upgrade).
 • Reapply in 2–4 weeks depending on infestation response.
 Step 2: Irrigation Retrofit
 • Decommission porous pipe system due to calcification.
 • Install misting irrigation with:
 • Fine droplet nozzles (anti-clog)
 • 2m spacing approx
 • Update timer with app operated for control from inside property
Pathways
Option A: Targeted Revival (Phased)
 • Control leatherjackets (local contractor) and upgrade irrigation.
 • Repair and replant only the worst-hit areas this year.
 • Review progress after 6 months
Option B: Full Refresh
 • Strip entire roof surface.
 • Apply nematodes (local contractor).
 • Replant uniformly with new sedum blankets and install new misting infrastructure.
